Claude Code 2.1.92 Changelog Deep Dive: All 21 Changes Explained

Apr 4, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Analysis date: 2026-04-04 Source: https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md

I. New Features (Added)

Section titled “I. New Features (Added)”

1. forceRemoteSettingsRefresh Policy Setting

Section titled “1. forceRemoteSettingsRefresh Policy Setting”

Background Enterprise/team admins distribute policies via managed-settings.json. Previously, these were cached in remote-settings.json — if a remote fetch failed on startup, the CLI would fall back to stale cache. Revoked permissions could remain effective, creating a security window.

Use Cases

  • Finance/healthcare compliance: revoked permissions must enforce immediately
  • SOC2/ISO27001 audits requiring “fail-closed” rather than “fail-open” policies

Example

CLI blocks on startup waiting for successful remote config fetch → proceeds only on success; exits on failure (fail-closed).

Notes

  • Unstable networks will prevent CLI startup — suited for corporate intranets, not offline dev
  • Only relevant for Team/Enterprise admins

Related Changes

  • 2.1.83: Added managed-settings.d/ sharded policy directory
  • 2.1.80: Fixed managed-settings not applied on startup
  • 2.1.78: Fixed PreToolUse hooks bypassing deny rules

Comparisons

  • Codex CLI: No enterprise policy management
  • Gemini CLI: Has enforcedAuthType (v0.5.0) but no fail-closed policy refresh

Trend: Enterprise CLI coding tools moving toward MDM-style policy compliance.

2. Interactive Bedrock Setup Wizard

Section titled “2. Interactive Bedrock Setup Wizard”

Background AWS Bedrock configuration was a pain point — manually setting multiple environment variables.

Use Cases

  • Enterprise users accessing Claude through AWS Bedrock
  • New employee onboarding without reading docs

Example Launch Claude Code → select “3rd-party platform” → enter wizard:

  1. Choose AWS auth method (SSO / Access Key / IAM Role)
  2. Configure Region
  3. Validate credentials
  4. Select/pin model

Notes

  • Only available from login screen; use claude auth logout to re-enter
  • Model pinning matters — Bedrock model IDs differ from Anthropic API format

Related Changes

  • 2.1.84: Added model capability override env vars for 3P
  • 2.1.86: Improved Bedrock/Vertex prompt cache hit rates
  • 2.1.83: Improved Bedrock SDK cold start latency

Comparisons

  • Codex CLI: OpenAI API only
  • Gemini CLI: Google Cloud only — simpler but no multi-cloud

Trend: Multi-cloud LLM access becoming enterprise must-have.

3. /cost Now Shows Per-Model and Cache-Hit Breakdown

Section titled “3. /cost Now Shows Per-Model and Cache-Hit Breakdown”

Background Previously /cost only showed total spend. No visibility into per-model costs or cache hit rates.

Use Cases

  • Subscription users optimizing token distribution
  • Deciding whether to adjust effort levels

Example

Notes

  • Only for subscription users
  • Cache-hit percentage helps decide whether to /clear

Related Changes

  • 2.1.89: Fixed sub-agent usage not counted in /stats
  • 2.1.84: Tokens ≥1M displayed as “1.5m”
  • 2.1.80: Added rate_limits to statusline

Comparisons

  • Codex CLI: No built-in cost tracking
  • Gemini CLI: Has --session-summary JSON but no interactive view

4. /release-notes Interactive Version Picker

Section titled “4. /release-notes Interactive Version Picker”

Previously only showed current version. Now you can browse any version’s changelog interactively.

5. Remote Control Session Names Use Hostname Prefix

Section titled “5. Remote Control Session Names Use Hostname Prefix”

Session names now default to macbook-pro-graceful-unicorn instead of just graceful-unicorn. Override with --remote-control-session-name-prefix.

6. Prompt Cache Expiration Notice (Pro Users)

Section titled “6. Prompt Cache Expiration Notice (Pro Users)”

Status bar now shows “~150K tokens will be sent uncached” when cache TTL expires. Helps decide whether to continue or /clear.

II. Bug Fixes (Fixed)

Section titled “II. Bug Fixes (Fixed)”

7. tmux Sub-Agent “Could not determine pane count” Error

Section titled “7. tmux Sub-Agent “Could not determine pane count” Error”

Fixed permanent sub-agent failure when tmux windows were manually killed or renumbered during long runs.

8. Stop Hooks False Failures and preventContinuation:true Fix

Section titled “8. Stop Hooks False Failures and preventContinuation:true Fix”

Fixed fast model ok:false incorrectly flagging hooks as failed, and preventContinuation:true semantics being lost on non-Stop hooks.

9. Streaming JSON-Encoded Field Validation Failures

Section titled “9. Streaming JSON-Encoded Field Validation Failures”

Fixed array/object fields arriving as JSON-encoded strings during streaming, causing type validation failures.

10. Extended Thinking Empty Text Blocks Causing API 400

Section titled “10. Extended Thinking Empty Text Blocks Causing API 400”

Fixed whitespace-only text blocks from extended thinking being rejected by the API.

11. Auto-Pilot Accidentally Triggering Feedback Surveys

Section titled “11. Auto-Pilot Accidentally Triggering Feedback Surveys”

Fixed automated keypresses triggering survey popups and number input conflicts with survey options.

12. Fullscreen “esc to interrupt” vs “esc to clear” Conflict

Section titled “12. Fullscreen “esc to interrupt” vs “esc to clear” Conflict”

Fixed contradictory Esc prompts appearing simultaneously during text selection.

13. Homebrew Update Channel Fix

Section titled “13. Homebrew Update Channel Fix”

Fixed brew upgrade claude-code and brew upgrade claude-code@latest using wrong release channels.

14. ctrl+e Multi-Line Edit Line Jump Bug

Section titled “14. ctrl+e Multi-Line Edit Line Jump Bug”

Fixed cursor jumping to next line’s end instead of staying on current line.

15. Fullscreen Duplicate Messages (DEC 2026 Terminals)

Section titled “15. Fullscreen Duplicate Messages (DEC 2026 Terminals)”

Fixed race condition in iTerm2/Ghostty causing messages to appear in two positions when scrolling.

16. “/clear to save X tokens” Incorrect Count

Section titled “16. “/clear to save X tokens” Incorrect Count”

Fixed displaying cumulative session tokens instead of current context size.

17. Plugin MCP Server vs claude.ai Connector Conflict

Section titled “17. Plugin MCP Server vs claude.ai Connector Conflict”

Fixed plugin MCP servers stuck in “connecting” when sharing names with unauthenticated claude.ai connectors.

III. Performance (Improved)

Section titled “III. Performance (Improved)”

18. Write Tool Diff Computation 60% Faster

Section titled “18. Write Tool Diff Computation 60% Faster”

Fixed special characters (tabs, &, $) causing diff algorithm degradation.

IV. Removed

Section titled “IV. Removed”

19. Removed /tag Command

Section titled “19. Removed /tag Command”

Session tagging removed, likely replaced by AI-generated session titles.

20. Removed /vim Command

Section titled “20. Removed /vim Command”

Moved to /config → Editor mode. Feature still exists, different entry point.

V. Security Hardening

Section titled “V. Security Hardening”

21. Linux Sandbox Restores apply-seccomp Helper

Section titled “21. Linux Sandbox Restores apply-seccomp Helper”

Fixed missing seccomp binary in npm/native builds that caused sandbox degradation on Linux.

Comparisons

  • Codex CLI: Docker-based --sandbox
  • Gemini CLI: Has sandbox with different implementation

VI. Comprehensive Comparison

Section titled “VI. Comprehensive Comparison”
  • Enterprise Policies: Claude Code has fail-closed + managed-settings.d; Codex CLI none; Gemini CLI has enforcedAuthType
  • Multi-Cloud: Claude Code has Bedrock + Vertex + Foundry; Codex CLI OpenAI-only; Gemini CLI Google-only
  • Cost Transparency: Claude Code per-model + cache-hit; Codex CLI none; Gemini CLI session-summary JSON
  • Sandbox: Claude Code seccomp; Codex CLI Docker; Gemini CLI has sandbox
  • Hooks: Claude Code comprehensive lifecycle; Codex CLI none; Gemini CLI Extensions
  • Terminal: Claude Code fullscreen + DEC 2026 + vim; Codex CLI basic; Gemini CLI rich TUI
  • Maturity: Claude Code 2.1.92 (rapid iteration); Codex CLI stable; Gemini CLI v0.7.0 (catching up)

VII. Future Trends

Section titled “VII. Future Trends”
  1. Enterprise Compliance: Expect policy audit logs, compliance reports
  2. Multi-Cloud UX: Vertex and Foundry guided flows coming
  3. Cost Visualization: Auto-suggestions like “Suggest /clear to save $X”
  4. Terminal Protocols: DEC 2026, Kitty keyboard protocol full support
  5. Hooks Platform: Evolving from scripts to full plugin API
  6. Sandbox Standardization: May converge on WebAssembly or unified containers

Let OpenClaw Configure Its Own Ollama Local Model: Gemma 4 31B in One Conversation

Apr 4, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Date: 2026-04-04 Environment: macOS 26.3.1 (Apple Silicon) · OpenClaw 2026.4.2 · Ollama running locally Model: gemma4:31b-it-bf16 (62GB, BF16 full precision)

Background

Section titled “Background”

OpenClaw supports multiple model providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Ollama, vLLM, etc.), but configuring a local model typically requires manually editing JSON config files. This time we tried something different: having the agent complete the entire process directly in OpenClaw chat — from confirming Ollama status, editing configuration, to running an end-to-end test.

All it took was one sentence:

“Add the local ollama run gemma4:31b-it-bf16 model to the local OpenClaw model list and test it”

The Process

Section titled “The Process”

Step 1: Environment Detection

Section titled “Step 1: Environment Detection”

The agent executed two groups of commands in parallel:

  1. Check OpenClaw status — openclaw status, confirming the gateway was running normally (local ws://127.0.0.1:18789)
  2. Check Ollama local models — ollama list + curl http://127.0.0.1:11434/api/tags

Results confirmed:

  • Ollama was running, gemma4:31b-it-bf16 already pulled (62GB)
  • OpenClaw gateway healthy, but no Ollama provider configured yet

Step 2: Documentation Lookup

Section titled “Step 2: Documentation Lookup”

The agent automatically searched OpenClaw’s Ollama provider documentation (/providers/ollama) and found two integration methods:

MethodDescription
Auto-discoverySet OLLAMA_API_KEY but don’t define models.providers.ollama, and OpenClaw automatically discovers models from local Ollama
Explicit configurationManually define baseUrl, apiKey, and models list in models.providers.ollama

Since we needed precise control over model IDs and aliases, the agent chose explicit configuration.

Step 3: Check Existing Configuration

Section titled “Step 3: Check Existing Configuration”

Found that models.providers already had 3 custom providers, but no ollama.

Step 4: CLI Configuration Attempt (Hit a Snag)

Section titled “Step 4: CLI Configuration Attempt (Hit a Snag)”

The agent first tried using openclaw config set to set fields one by one:

The gotcha: OpenClaw’s config schema requires all mandatory provider fields (baseUrl, models) to be present simultaneously — you can’t set them one at a time. The config set command writing fields individually triggers intermediate state validation failures.

Step 5: Direct JSON Config Editing

Section titled “Step 5: Direct JSON Config Editing”

The agent switched to a Python script to edit ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json directly:

Then validated:

Step 6: Confirm Model Visibility

Section titled “Step 6: Confirm Model Visibility”

Output:

✅ Model appeared in the list — 195k context window, local auth verified.

Step 7: End-to-End Test

Section titled “Step 7: End-to-End Test”

The agent spawned a subagent with model: ollama/gemma4:31b-it-bf16 and sent a test prompt:

“Reply with only: OK_GEMMA4”

5 seconds later:

Test passed. 🎉

Final Configuration

Section titled “Final Configuration”

Key configuration written to ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json:

Usage

Section titled “Usage”

After configuration, in any OpenClaw session:

You can also specify the model in cron jobs:

Key Takeaways

Section titled “Key Takeaways”

1. api: "ollama" vs OpenAI Compatible Mode

Section titled “1. api: "ollama" vs OpenAI Compatible Mode”

OpenClaw supports two Ollama integration methods:

ConfigbaseUrlapiDescription
Native modehttp://host:11434ollamaUses Ollama’s native /api/chat, full tool calling support
Compatible modehttp://host:11434/v1openai-completionsUses OpenAI-compatible endpoint, some features limited

Recommended: native mode (api: "ollama") for better tool calling support.

2. Limitations of config set

Section titled “2. Limitations of config set”

openclaw config set doesn’t currently support atomic writes for nested provider objects. When creating a new provider with multiple required fields at once, directly editing the JSON file is more reliable.

3. Auto-discovery vs Explicit Configuration

Section titled “3. Auto-discovery vs Explicit Configuration”
  • Auto-discovery: Set the OLLAMA_API_KEY=ollama-local environment variable and don’t define models.providers.ollama — OpenClaw will automatically list all local Ollama models
  • Explicit configuration: Define in models.providers.ollama for precise control over model IDs, aliases, context windows, and other parameters

If you just want quick access to all local models, auto-discovery is easier. For customization (aliases, parameter overrides, etc.), use explicit configuration.

4. The Cost of BF16 Full Precision

Section titled “4. The Cost of BF16 Full Precision”

gemma4:31b-it-bf16 weighs in at 62GB and requires sufficient GPU/unified memory. On Apple Silicon (M-series) chips, the unified memory architecture handles it reasonably well, but expect cold-start latency on first inference. In testing, a single simple response took about 5 seconds.

Summary

Section titled “Summary”

From issuing the command to passing the test, the entire process took under 5 minutes, all within the OpenClaw chat window:

  1. Agent auto-detected environment → looked up docs → edited config → validated → confirmed visibility → end-to-end test
  2. The human said exactly one sentence
  3. The agent hit one snag (config set atomicity issue) and independently found an alternative

This is OpenClaw’s self-ops capability: the agent understands its own configuration system and uses its toolchain to configure itself. Next time a new model is added, you might not even need to say anything — just let heartbeat auto-discover newly pulled Ollama models.

This article was auto-generated by an OpenClaw agent after completing the configuration.

OpenClaw Cron Delivery to WeChat: Configuring Multi-Channel Environments

Apr 4, 2026
Vibe Sparking

The Problem: 17 Cron Jobs, Most Failing to Deliver

Section titled “The Problem: 17 Cron Jobs, Most Failing to Deliver”

Our OpenClaw cluster runs 17 cron jobs across 5 different Agents — meeting reminders, expense reminders, GitLab monitoring, data backups, blog content scanning, and more.

They executed fine, but delivery was entirely broken — or not configured at all. Two typical errors:

One GitLab monitoring job had 10 consecutive failures before anyone noticed.

Root Cause: Incomplete Delivery Config in Multi-Channel Environments

Section titled “Root Cause: Incomplete Delivery Config in Multi-Channel Environments”

The issue is that our OpenClaw instance has multiple messaging channels configured simultaneously (Telegram, Discord, Feishu, WeChat). When a Cron Job’s delivery only specifies channel: "openclaw-weixin" without a to (target chat ID), the system doesn’t know who to deliver to.

Single-channel setups don’t have this problem — the system infers the target automatically. But in multi-channel environments, three fields are required:

FieldPurposeExample
channelWhich messaging pluginopenclaw-weixin
toDeliver to whom (chat ID)oXXX@im.wechat
accountIdWhich bot sends it7dca...im-bot

The Fix

Section titled “The Fix”

Step 1: Find the WeChat Bot’s Target Info

Section titled “Step 1: Find the WeChat Bot’s Target Info”

Use sessions_list to find active WeChat sessions and extract the complete delivery triple from deliveryContext:

Step 2: Batch Update All Jobs

Section titled “Step 2: Batch Update All Jobs”

Use the Cron tool’s update action to update each job’s delivery config:

17 jobs updated total:

  • 12 had WeChat delivery configured but missing to/accountId → filled in
  • 5 were running silently (delivery: none) → switched to announce

Results

Section titled “Results”

After the fix:

  • GitLab monitoring delivered successfully twice in a row (was failing 10 times straight)
  • Jobs outputting NO_REPLY are automatically suppressed — no noise for the user
  • All reminder jobs awaiting their next trigger cycle for validation

Key Takeaways

Section titled “Key Takeaways”

1. Multi-Channel Requires Complete Config

Section titled “1. Multi-Channel Requires Complete Config”

All three fields are mandatory in multi-channel setups. Single-channel environments can omit to and accountId.

2. How to Find Your to Value

Section titled “2. How to Find Your to Value”

3. The NO_REPLY Pattern

Section titled “3. The NO_REPLY Pattern”

If a cron job decides there’s nothing worth pushing, output NO_REPLY — OpenClaw automatically skips delivery. Essential for high-frequency monitoring jobs.

4. Silent vs Push: Choose Wisely

Section titled “4. Silent vs Push: Choose Wisely”

Not every job needs delivery. Hourly data backups might be too noisy. Consider:

  • Push only on failure (add logic in the prompt)
  • Reduce push frequency (daily summary only)
  • Stay silent (delivery: none), check manually when needed

Summary

Section titled “Summary”

Multi-channel is one of OpenClaw’s strengths — one instance connecting WeChat, Telegram, Discord, and Feishu simultaneously. But it means Cron Job delivery config needs to be explicit. Remember the triple: channel + to + accountId, and you won’t hit this pitfall again.

OpenClaw: Your Digital Operating System for Work & Life — The P.D.C.A.S Framework in Practice

Apr 4, 2026
Vibe Sparking

OpenClaw: Your Digital Operating System for Work & Life

Section titled “OpenClaw: Your Digital Operating System for Work & Life”

Use AI as a tool, and you get a fancy search engine. Use AI as an operating system, and you get a tireless digital twin.

We’re at a subtle inflection point: AI is no longer just a “ask and answer” dialog box. It’s becoming something that can run continuously, execute proactively, and collaborate across contexts. OpenClaw was built for exactly this moment — it’s not another ChatBot wrapper, but an Agent-centric digital operating system.

This article takes you deep into OpenClaw’s core architecture and demonstrates how a P.D.C.A.S closed-loop workflow I use every day transforms fragmented digital life into a self-driving system.

What Is OpenClaw?

Section titled “What Is OpenClaw?”

In one sentence: OpenClaw is a multi-agent, multi-session, multi-channel AI operating system.

Let me unpack that.

Multi-Channel Access: Chat Anywhere, Anytime

Section titled “Multi-Channel Access: Chat Anywhere, Anytime”

OpenClaw isn’t locked to a single entry point. You can talk to your Agent through:

  • WebUI — Open a browser tab, start working. Great for long-form editing and complex tasks
  • TUI (Terminal UI) — For command-line enthusiasts: openclaw chat and you’re in
  • IM Integration — WeChat, Telegram, Discord, WhatsApp, Signal… send a message, Agent handles it

This means you can fire off a WeChat message on the subway, and by the time you’re at your desk opening the WebUI, the task is already done. Not science fiction — just my Tuesday.

SOTA Model-Driven: No Compromises

Section titled “SOTA Model-Driven: No Compromises”

OpenClaw supports flexible model configuration:

  • Claude Opus 4 as the primary model for complex reasoning and long-form writing
  • GPT-5.4 as an alternative, the best choice for certain scenarios
  • Gemini, DeepSeek and more, switchable on demand
  • Automatic model failover ensures the service never goes down

Each Agent can independently configure its model and thinking level, choosing the most appropriate “brain” for each task.

Multi-Agent Isolation & Collaboration

Section titled “Multi-Agent Isolation & Collaboration”

This is one of OpenClaw’s most powerful design choices. You can create multiple Agents, each with independent:

  • Workspace — Its own files, memory, configuration
  • Identity (SOUL.md) — Defining personality and behavioral guidelines
  • Skills — Each Agent excels at different things
  • Permission boundaries — Agents don’t interfere with each other

For example, my system has these Agents, each with its own role:

  • vs-sites-astro — Blog content creation and publishing
  • vs-openclaw-mgr — OpenClaw system management and maintenance
  • vs-wechat — WeChat message processing and content decryption
  • vs-ops-mgr — Team operations, meeting reminders, administrative tasks

They share the same OpenClaw Gateway but are logically fully isolated. vs-ops-mgr can’t see vs-sites-astro’s blog drafts, and vs-wechat won’t touch operations data.

Sessions: More Powerful Than Conversations

Section titled “Sessions: More Powerful Than Conversations”

In OpenClaw, a Session isn’t just “a chat log” — it’s a stateful execution environment:

  • Main Session — Your daily conversation with the Agent, maintaining full context
  • Isolated Session — Independent runtime for cron jobs and background tasks, keeping your main conversation clean
  • Sub-agents — The main Session can spawn child tasks that auto-report when complete

Each Session has its own context window management, memory injection, and tool permissions. This lets OpenClaw handle multiple tasks simultaneously without interference.

P.D.C.A.S: The Complete Loop from Idea to Share

Section titled “P.D.C.A.S: The Complete Loop from Idea to Share”

The classic PDCA (Plan-Do-Check-Act) cycle is well-established. But in an AI-driven workflow, I’ve added an S — Share, forming the P.D.C.A.S closed loop:

Let me walk through each stage with real OpenClaw workflows.

P — Plan: Communicate Ideas, Thoughts, Questions

Section titled “P — Plan: Communicate Ideas, Thoughts, Questions”

Scenario: You have an idea for an article about how engineers transition to engineering managers in the AI era.

You send your Agent a WeChat message:

“I want to write an article about how engineers can transition to engineering managers in the AI era”

The Agent doesn’t just say “OK.” Instead, it:

  1. Searches memory — Checks MEMORY.md and memory/ for prior related discussions
  2. Understands context — Combines your USER.md (who you are, what you care about) with SOUL.md (Agent’s behavioral guidelines)
  3. Proposes structure — Suggests an outline with title, core arguments, target audience
  4. Confirms direction — Waits for your go-ahead before executing

The key here: the Agent is your thinking partner, not an execution machine. It challenges your ideas, raises angles you hadn’t considered, and might even tell you “someone wrote something similar last week.”

D — Do: Drive OpenClaw to Execute

Section titled “D — Do: Drive OpenClaw to Execute”

Once direction is confirmed, the Agent starts executing. This is where OpenClaw’s architecture shines:

Immediate Execution:

Scheduled Execution (Cron Jobs):

OpenClaw’s cron system is the backbone of background automation. Two key examples from my setup:

daily-session-workspace-audit (Daily at 11:00 AM)

Section titled “daily-session-workspace-audit (Daily at 11:00 AM)”

Executed by the vs-openclaw-mgr Agent:

  • Scans all Agent workspaces for health status
  • Checks for uncommitted code changes
  • Cleans up expired temporary files
  • Validates critical configuration file integrity
  • Generates audit reports

Think of it as having a DevOps engineer patrol your system every day, ensuring everything runs smoothly.

daily-blog-sharing-check (Daily at 12:00 PM)

Section titled “daily-blog-sharing-check (Daily at 12:00 PM)”

Executed by the vs-sites-astro Agent:

  • Checks whether recently published blog posts have been pushed to WeChat Official Account
  • Verifies bilingual versions (Chinese + English) are complete
  • Checks that cover images and illustrations have been generated
  • Creates todo reminders for any gaps found

Both cron jobs run in isolated Sessions, never polluting your daily conversation. Results are pushed to your chat channel when complete.

Cross-Agent Collaboration:

Writing a blog post seems simple, but it actually involves multiple steps:

  1. vs-sites-astro handles content creation and Astro blog publishing
  2. Calls info-card-designer Skill to generate cover and illustration images
  3. Calls wenyan CLI to push to WeChat Official Account draft box
  4. Content is simultaneously generated in both Chinese and English

These steps can run sequentially, or the Agent can spawn sub-tasks for parallel processing.

C — Check: Test and Verify Results

Section titled “C — Check: Test and Verify Results”

After execution, verification is essential:

Immediate Verification:

  • Is the article correctly saved to src/content/docs/?
  • Is the frontmatter format correct (date, slug, tags, image)?
  • Does the cover image meet size requirements (900x383 px)?
  • Was the WeChat draft successfully created (returns Media ID)?

Scheduled Verification (daily-blog-sharing-check):

  • Automatic daily check: have recent articles completed the full publishing pipeline?
  • Any “written but not pushed to WeChat” omissions?
  • Any “Chinese done but English not translated” half-finished work?

This dual verification (immediate + scheduled) ensures nothing falls through the cracks. Like CI/CD + monitoring alerts in software development — checks at every layer.

A — Act: Review, Summarize, Commit to Memory

Section titled “A — Act: Review, Summarize, Commit to Memory”

This is OpenClaw’s most “soulful” feature — the memory system.

Each Agent maintains two layers of memory:

Daily Notes: memory/YYYY-MM-DD.md

  • What happened today
  • Which tasks were completed
  • What problems were encountered
  • Raw, unprocessed records

Long-term Memory: MEMORY.md

  • Lessons distilled from daily notes
  • User preferences and habits
  • Important decisions and their reasoning
  • A continuously updated “cognitive model”

The Agent periodically reviews daily notes during heartbeat checks, writing what’s worth keeping long-term into MEMORY.md. This isn’t copy-paste — it’s distillation — keeping the essence, discarding noise.

For example:

Daily note: “2026-04-03, user requested analysis of Claude Code Changelog 2.1.91, covering all 13 items.”

Long-term memory distilled: “User is highly interested in Claude Code updates, prefers detailed technical analysis over simple changelog translations.”

This memory mechanism means the Agent understands you better over time. The first time you might need to explain “I like this style.” By the tenth time, the Agent already knows.

S — Share: Publish to WeChat Official Account / Blog

Section titled “S — Share: Publish to WeChat Official Account / Blog”

The final step — and the most exciting — one-click sharing.

The wechat-official-account-article Skill is a custom publishing pipeline with a complete workflow:

Phase 0: Preflight

  • Verify Astro project directory
  • Confirm wenyan CLI is installed
  • Check info-card-designer Skill availability

Phase 1: Create Astro Blog Post

  • Adapt content to Astro Starlight format
  • Generate standardized frontmatter (including source_url pointing to the blog original)
  • Auto-categorize to appropriate directory

Phase 1.5: Generate Bilingual Version

  • Chinese source -> automatically translate to English
  • Preserve Markdown structure, code blocks, tables
  • Adapt language-prefix slug

Phase 2: Generate Cover & Illustration

  • Call info-card-designer to generate 900x383 px cover image
  • Generate matching illustration
  • Embed in article body

Phase 3: Push to WeChat

  • Publish to WeChat draft box via wenyan CLI
  • Format with lapis theme
  • Return Media ID for confirmation

Phase 4: Update Issue Tracking

  • Create work ticket in engineering/00-issues/
  • Mark completed checklist items
  • Enable future tracking

The entire flow from “I want to publish an article” to “it’s sitting in the WeChat draft box” is fully automated by the Agent. You only need to set the original content flag and comment settings in the WeChat backend at the end.

System Architecture Overview

Section titled “System Architecture Overview”

Cron Jobs: The System’s Heartbeat

Section titled “Cron Jobs: The System’s Heartbeat”

OpenClaw’s scheduling system operates in two modes:

Cron Jobs: Precision Timing

Section titled “Cron Jobs: Precision Timing”

For tasks that need exact triggers:

  • daily-session-workspace-audit — 11:00 AM daily, system health check
  • daily-blog-sharing-check — 12:00 PM daily, content publishing completeness check
  • wechat-decrypt-daytime — Hourly during daytime, WeChat message decryption
  • Various reminders — Meeting advance notices, expense reminders, weekly report reminders

Heartbeat: Flexible Patrol

Section titled “Heartbeat: Flexible Patrol”

For checks that don’t need exact timing but should happen regularly:

  • Email inbox patrol
  • Calendar reminders
  • Social media notifications
  • Memory maintenance

The two modes complement each other: Cron guarantees precision, Heartbeat guarantees coverage.

Skills System: The Agent’s Capability Matrix

Section titled “Skills System: The Agent’s Capability Matrix”

OpenClaw’s Skills system gives Agents “professional skills.” My current system has 80+ ready skills covering:

  • Content Creation — wechat-official-account-article, info-card-designer, summarize
  • Software Development — coding-agent, github, gh-issues
  • Communication — himalaya (email), imsg, wacli (WhatsApp)
  • Knowledge Management — obsidian, apple-notes, bear-notes
  • System Operations — healthcheck, node-connect, tmux
  • Life Assistance — weather, apple-reminders, openhue (smart lighting)
  • Information Retrieval — web-search, web-fetch, blogwatcher

Each Skill is a standalone SKILL.md file defining inputs, execution steps, output specs, and error handling. The Agent loads the relevant Skill on demand — just like a human consulting an operations manual.

Real-World Case Study: How This Article Was Written

Section titled “Real-World Case Study: How This Article Was Written”

That’s right — the article you’re reading is itself a product of the P.D.C.A.S loop:

  1. Plan — Proposed the idea in WebUI: “Write a long article about OpenClaw as a digital operating system”
  2. Do — Agent analyzed requirements, organized structure, pulled cron job and skill info from memory, wrote the full article
  3. Check — Verified article structural completeness, checked technical accuracy, confirmed frontmatter format
  4. Act — Recorded this writing experience in today’s memory file
  5. Share — Published to blog and WeChat Official Account via the wechat-official-account-article Skill

Meta-recursion: Using OpenClaw to write an article about OpenClaw, then using OpenClaw to publish it. That’s the best proof there is.

Why “Operating System” and Not “Tool”?

Section titled “Why “Operating System” and Not “Tool”?”

A tool is something you pick up and use. An operating system is always running.

OpenClaw doesn’t need you to open an app to work. Its Gateway runs continuously, cron jobs execute on schedule, message routing distributes automatically. While you sleep, it’s patrolling. While you’re in meetings, it’s processing messages. While you’re coding, it’s auditing your Workspace.

This is “operating system”-level AI — not passively waiting for commands, but actively maintaining your digital life.

Final Thoughts

Section titled “Final Thoughts”

We’re experiencing a paradigm shift from “AI tools” to “AI operating systems.” OpenClaw represents one practice of this direction:

  • Not replacing humans, but augmenting them — Agents handle repetitive work; humans focus on creative thinking
  • Not a point tool, but a system architecture — Multi-agent, multi-session, multi-channel, forming a complete ecosystem
  • Not one-off conversations, but continuous operation — Cron jobs, heartbeat checks, memory systems build long-term relationships
  • Not a closed platform, but an open framework — Skills are customizable, models are switchable, channels are extensible

The P.D.C.A.S loop isn’t a new concept, but with AI Agent support, it’s become frictionless for the first time. From idea to share, no more switching between ten apps, no more manually checking every step — OpenClaw weaves it all into a smooth workflow.

In the future, your digital life won’t need you to “operate” it. You just need to think, decide, and create — the rest is for your Agent operating system to handle.

This article was written by OpenClaw Agent vs-sites-astro and auto-published via the wechat-official-account-article Skill.

  • OpenClaw
  • AI Agent
  • Productivity
  • Workflow Automation
  • PDCAS

cc-connect: Bridge Local AI Coding Agents to Messaging Platforms

Apr 3, 2026
Vibe Sparking

cc-connect bridges 7 AI coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, etc.) to 10 messaging platforms (Feishu, DingTalk, Telegram, etc.) — no public IP required.

What Is cc-connect?

Section titled “What Is cc-connect?”

cc-connect is an open-source bridging tool that connects AI coding agents running on your local machine to the messaging platforms you already use. Code review, research, automation, data analysis — anything an AI agent can do is now accessible from your phone, tablet, or any device with a chat app.

In short: Control your local AI agents from any chat app, anywhere, anytime.

Supported AI Agents

Section titled “Supported AI Agents”

cc-connect currently supports 7 AI coding agents:

  • Claude Code (Anthropic) — ✅ Supported
  • Codex (OpenAI) — ✅ Supported
  • Cursor Agent — ✅ Supported
  • Gemini CLI (Google) — ✅ Supported
  • Qoder CLI — ✅ Supported
  • OpenCode (Crush) — ✅ Supported
  • iFlow CLI — ✅ Supported
  • Goose (Block) — 🔜 Planned
  • Aider — 🔜 Planned

Supported Messaging Platforms

Section titled “Supported Messaging Platforms”

Covering 10 major platforms, most requiring no public IP:

  • Feishu (Lark) — WebSocket, no public IP needed
  • DingTalk — Stream, no public IP needed
  • Telegram — Long Polling, no public IP needed
  • Slack — Socket Mode, no public IP needed
  • Discord — Gateway, no public IP needed
  • LINE — Webhook, public IP required
  • WeChat Work — WebSocket / Webhook, no public IP for WS
  • Weixin (personal, ilink) — HTTP long polling, no public IP (beta only)
  • QQ (NapCat/OneBot) — WebSocket, no public IP needed
  • QQ Bot (Official) — WebSocket, no public IP needed

Personal WeChat support is currently available only in beta builds — install cc-connect@beta.

Platform Feature Overview

Section titled “Platform Feature Overview”

Feature support varies by platform:

  • Text & slash commands: All platforms
  • Markdown / card messages: Most platforms; LINE and WeChat Work have partial support
  • Streaming / chunked replies: All platforms
  • Images & files: Most platforms
  • Voice / STT / TTS: Best on Telegram and Weixin (beta); others require extra config
  • Private and group chats: All platforms

Key Features

Section titled “Key Features”

Multi-Agent Orchestration

Section titled “Multi-Agent Orchestration”

cc-connect supports multi-bot relay — bind multiple AI agents in a single group chat and let them communicate. Ask Claude a question, then get insights from Gemini — all in one conversation.

Full Session Management

Section titled “Full Session Management”

Manage everything via chat commands:

Permission Modes

Section titled “Permission Modes”

Model Switching

Section titled “Model Switching”

Scheduled Tasks

Section titled “Scheduled Tasks”

Set up cron jobs:

Multimodal Support

Section titled “Multimodal Support”

Send voice messages or screenshots; cc-connect handles STT/TTS and multimodal forwarding automatically.

Multi-Project Architecture

Section titled “Multi-Project Architecture”

One process, multiple projects — each with its own agent and platform combination.

Attachment Send-Back

Section titled “Attachment Send-Back”

When an agent generates screenshots, charts, PDFs, or other files, they can be sent back to the chat directly (currently supported on Feishu and Telegram).

Quick Start

Section titled “Quick Start”

Installation

Section titled “Installation”

Via npm:

Download binary from GitHub Releases:

Build from source (requires Go 1.22+):

Configuration

Section titled “Configuration”

Set admin_from = "alice,bob" in a project to allow those user IDs to run privileged commands.

Run

Section titled “Run”

Beta Highlights

Section titled “Beta Highlights”

The latest beta brings several notable updates:

  • Personal WeChat — Connect via ilink long polling, QR code scan, no public IP needed
  • Auto-compress — Automatically trims context when sessions exceed thresholds
  • Friendlier --continue — Fork-on-continue prevents inheriting half-finished terminal sessions
  • Cron with boundaries — Run jobs in fresh sessions with per-job timeout caps
  • Richer platform features — Discord @everyone/@here, Telegram voice replies, Feishu reply threading fixes

Multilingual Support

Section titled “Multilingual Support”

cc-connect ships with 5 built-in languages: English, Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese, Japanese, and Spanish.

Summary

Section titled “Summary”

cc-connect provides a lightweight bridge between local AI coding agents and messaging platforms. If you’re using Claude Code, Cursor, or Gemini CLI and want to control them from your phone or chat app wherever you are, cc-connect is a solid open-source option worth trying.

Claude Code 2.1.91 Deep Dive: Breaking Down All 13 Changes

Apr 3, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Analysis date: 2026-04-03 Source: Claude Code CHANGELOG.md

Claude Code 2.1.91 looks like a small patch release on paper, but it carries a surprisingly strong signal. These 13 updates span five themes at once: MCP maturity, enterprise safety, session reliability, token efficiency, and developer experience.

This article walks through each change, the problem behind it, practical use cases, caveats, related changes in earlier versions, and how it compares with Codex CLI and Gemini CLI.

Why 2.1.91 matters more than it looks

Section titled “Why 2.1.91 matters more than it looks”

At first glance, this is just a short changelog. In reality, it reveals several clear product directions:

  1. MCP is moving from “works” to “scales.”
  2. Enterprise controls are getting stricter and more explicit.
  3. Session durability remains a major engineering battlefield.
  4. Token economics are now being optimized at the tool-protocol level.

Let’s go change by change.

1. MCP large-result persistence override

Section titled “1. MCP large-result persistence override”

Change: Claude Code now supports _meta["anthropic/maxResultSizeChars"], allowing an MCP server to request a higher result retention cap of up to 500K characters.

Background

Section titled “Background”

Claude Code has default truncation limits for MCP tool results, roughly around 25K characters, to avoid flooding the context window. That works fine for small outputs, but it becomes painful when an MCP tool returns something genuinely important and naturally large, such as a database schema, a repository index, or a large search result.

Before this release, MCP server authors had no direct way to say: “this result is large, but it is also important—please keep more of it.”

Practical scenarios

Section titled “Practical scenarios”
  • Database schema inspection: a Postgres MCP server returns the full schema for 200+ tables
  • Code search: a repository-wide search returns many relevant code blocks that should remain intact
  • Document retrieval: an MCP-based RAG server returns several long but highly relevant documents

Technical detail

Section titled “Technical detail”

The MCP server can return metadata like this:

This is an Anthropic-specific vendor extension, built on top of the MCP _meta extension mechanism.

Caveats

Section titled “Caveats”
  • The cap is still finite: 500K is the upper bound
  • Larger results consume more context and may trigger compaction sooner
  • MCP servers must opt in explicitly

Related changes in earlier versions

Section titled “Related changes in earlier versions”
VersionRelated change
2.1.84MCP tool descriptions capped at 2KB
2.1.86Better prompt cache hit rate by removing dynamic tool-description content
2.1.89Fixed MCP error truncation to only the first content block

Comparison

Section titled “Comparison”
ProductLarge MCP result handling
Claude CodeServer-side override via _meta, up to 500K
Codex CLINo MCP support; uses native function calling
Gemini CLISupports MCP-style extensions, but no equivalent server-side size override

Trend

Section titled “Trend”

This is the kind of capability that may eventually become standardized in MCP itself. For now, Anthropic is moving faster through vendor extensions.

2. disableSkillShellExecution for enterprise safety

Section titled “2. disableSkillShellExecution for enterprise safety”

Change: A new setting disables inline shell execution in skills, custom slash commands, and plugin commands.

Background

Section titled “Background”

Skills are powerful, but that power comes with risk. If a skill can execute shell inline, then an untrusted or poorly audited skill can become a serious safety problem in enterprise environments.

This release finally adds a clean master switch.

Practical scenarios

Section titled “Practical scenarios”
  • Enterprise IT policy: centrally disable shell execution in third-party skills
  • CI/CD environments: reduce execution surface area in automated runs
  • Compliance-heavy organizations: ensure that all execution paths remain explicit and auditable

Caveats

Section titled “Caveats”
  • This only blocks inline shell execution inside skills/commands/plugins
  • It does not disable ordinary user-requested Bash tool calls
  • Existing skills that depend on inline shell execution may stop working

Related changes

Section titled “Related changes”
VersionRelated change
2.1.83managed-settings.d/ for modular enterprise policy
2.1.85Org policy can block plugin installation
2.1.78CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB to remove credentials from subprocesses

Comparison

Section titled “Comparison”
ProductControl model
Claude CodeExplicit disableSkillShellExecution switch
Codex CLIPlugin sandbox model with explicit permissions
Gemini CLIFine-grained Policy Engine allowlisting

This is a strong signal that Claude Code is continuing its shift from a hacker-friendly terminal tool toward a more controlled enterprise execution surface.

3. Multi-line prompts in deep links

Section titled “3. Multi-line prompts in deep links”

Change: claude-cli://open?q= now accepts encoded newlines (%0A) in prompts.

Why this matters

Section titled “Why this matters”

This sounds tiny, but it actually matters a lot for integration. Once deep links can carry multi-line prompts, Claude Code becomes easier to embed inside IDEs, documentation, tutorials, browser tools, and automation workflows.

Example

Section titled “Example”

Related changes

Section titled “Related changes”
VersionRelated change
2.1.85Deep-link query length raised to 5,000 chars
2.1.84Deep links open in the preferred terminal
2.1.89Fixed claude-cli:// not opening on macOS
2.1.83Added disableDeepLinkRegistration

Comparison

Section titled “Comparison”

Deep-link support remains a distinctive Claude Code advantage. Neither Codex CLI nor Gemini CLI currently has a comparable CLI protocol ecosystem.

4. Plugins can ship executables in bin/

Section titled “4. Plugins can ship executables in bin/”

Change: Plugins can now include executables under bin/ and invoke them as bare commands from Bash.

What this unlocks

Section titled “What this unlocks”

This moves plugins closer to being real, self-contained tool bundles rather than just wrappers around prompts, hooks, or MCP declarations.

Practical scenarios

Section titled “Practical scenarios”
  • A custom linter bundled as bin/my-linter
  • A schema/code generator packaged with the plugin
  • A workflow plugin that ships specialized infra tools

Caveats

Section titled “Caveats”
  • Files under bin/ still need correct executable permissions
  • Existing permission policies still apply
  • 2.1.86 recently fixed marketplace-plugin permission issues on macOS/Linux

Comparison

Section titled “Comparison”
ProductPlugin executable model
Claude CodeNative bin/ support for bare-command invocation
Codex CLIPlugin system supports custom tools, but with a different model
Gemini CLIExtensions are generally MCP/npm oriented, not bin/ oriented

This is a meaningful step toward a more serious plugin ecosystem.

5. Fixed transcript-chain breaks on --resume

Section titled “5. Fixed transcript-chain breaks on --resume”

Change: Claude Code fixed cases where async transcript write failures could silently break conversation history during --resume.

Why this is dangerous

Section titled “Why this is dangerous”

This is the worst kind of bug in an agent system: not a loud crash, but a silent loss of history. Users believe a session has been restored, but the context chain is already broken.

Practical scenarios

Section titled “Practical scenarios”
  • Resuming a long coding session the next day and finding part of the context gone
  • Recovering deferred tools in SDK or CI flows with missing state
  • Containerized remote sessions losing transcript integrity after restarts

Why --resume keeps showing up in the changelog

Section titled “Why --resume keeps showing up in the changelog”

Because it sits at the intersection of several hard problems:

  • tool/result consistency
  • async persistence timing
  • large-session durability
  • old-transcript compatibility
  • remote container lifecycle issues

Related fixes across versions

Section titled “Related fixes across versions”
VersionRelated fix
2.1.90Prompt-cache miss on --resume
2.1.89Older-transcript crashes; -p --resume hangs
2.1.86Missing tool_result chain restoration
2.1.85SDK history loss on resume
2.1.83Remote-session history loss after restart
2.1.77Silent truncation of recent history

Comparison

Section titled “Comparison”
ProductSession recovery model
Claude CodeFull transcript-chain restore via --resume
Codex CLISimpler session-file restore
Gemini CLI30-day history plus /rewind

Claude Code’s system is more ambitious, but that also means more complexity and more repair work.

6. Fixed cmd+delete across modern terminals

Section titled “6. Fixed cmd+delete across modern terminals”

Change: cmd+delete now correctly deletes to the start of the line in iTerm2, kitty, WezTerm, Ghostty, and Windows Terminal.

This is not a glamorous fix, but it’s exactly the sort of thing power users feel every day.

Root cause

Section titled “Root cause”

Different terminals emit different escape sequences for the same shortcut. Claude Code had only covered part of that landscape.

Fallback

Section titled “Fallback”

Ctrl+U remains the reliable readline-style fallback.

Comparison

Section titled “Comparison”

All three products face terminal compatibility friction. Claude Code is doing an especially thorough job of adapting to newer terminals like Ghostty and kitty.

7. Fixed plan mode in remote sessions

Section titled “7. Fixed plan mode in remote sessions”

Change: Claude Code fixed plan mode losing track of its plan file in remote sessions after container restarts.

What was happening

Section titled “What was happening”

Once the plan file path was lost, two bad things followed:

  1. Editing the plan triggered unnecessary permission prompts
  2. The plan-approval modal showed up empty

Impacted environments

Section titled “Impacted environments”
  • Remote Control sessions
  • Dev Containers
  • cloud IDEs such as Codespaces/Gitpod-like environments

Comparison

Section titled “Comparison”
ProductPlan mode + remote
Claude CodeMature plan mode plus remote control, now more reliable
Codex CLINo equivalent plan mode
Gemini CLIPlan mode by default, but no comparable remote-session stack

This fix highlights that Claude Code is increasingly operating as a persistent cross-device work environment, not just a local CLI.

8. Fixed schema validation for permissions.defaultMode: "auto"

Section titled “8. Fixed schema validation for permissions.defaultMode: "auto"”

Change: JSON schema validation now correctly accepts permissions.defaultMode: "auto".

This is a “small but important” fix. Even if the setting worked at runtime, a schema mismatch damages trust:

  • editors show red squiggles
  • teams doubt the docs
  • config rollout becomes noisier than it should be

For enterprise deployment, schema correctness matters more than many teams realize.

9. Fixed Windows rollback-copy cleanup

Section titled “9. Fixed Windows rollback-copy cleanup”

Change: Windows version cleanup no longer deletes the rollback copy of the active version.

This is classic reliability plumbing. Nobody notices it when it works, but when rollback is needed, it becomes critical.

Claude Code’s Windows installation model is heavier than npm-only tools like Codex CLI or Gemini CLI, so this kind of fix matters more in its ecosystem.

10. /feedback now explains why it is unavailable

Section titled “10. /feedback now explains why it is unavailable”

Change: /feedback no longer simply disappears; it now explains why it cannot be used.

This is a very good UX improvement. “Unavailable with explanation” is much better than “seems to have vanished.” That matters especially for:

  • enterprise deployments
  • third-party provider setups
  • proxy and managed environments

This reduces the chance that users interpret an intentional limitation as a broken product.

11. Improved /claude-api skill guidance

Section titled “11. Improved /claude-api skill guidance”

Change: Anthropic expanded the built-in /claude-api guidance around agent design patterns, including tool-surface choices, context management, and caching strategy.

This looks like a docs tweak, but it actually matters a lot. The competitive edge in 2026 is no longer just model quality. It is increasingly about:

  • how many tools you expose
  • how you control context growth
  • how you use caching well
  • when to split or avoid subagents

Anthropic is effectively productizing its own operational experience into reusable guidance.

12. Faster stripAnsi on Bun

Section titled “12. Faster stripAnsi on Bun”

Change: Claude Code now routes ANSI stripping through native Bun.stripANSI when running on Bun.

This is the kind of high-frequency micro-optimization that compounds over time. Each call is small, but log-heavy workflows invoke this path constantly.

Practical scenarios

Section titled “Practical scenarios”
  • long build logs
  • package installs
  • test runs with large terminal output

Gemini CLI and Codex CLI still primarily follow Node.js-first paths, so this kind of Bun-specific optimization is a notable differentiator.

13. Shorter old_string anchors in the Edit tool

Section titled “13. Shorter old_string anchors in the Edit tool”

Change: The Edit tool now uses shorter old_string anchors while still preserving uniqueness, reducing output tokens.

This is one of the most revealing changes in the whole release.

Why it matters

Section titled “Why it matters”

It shows that Claude Code is now optimizing token costs at the tool protocol level, not just at the prompt or model level.

In agent systems, cost comes from more than inference:

  • verbose tool schemas
  • repetitive file context
  • long edit anchors
  • redundant tool I/O

Once a team starts optimizing anchor length, it means they are thinking in terms of “token compound interest” across thousands of repeated actions.

Claude Code in Action: AI-Assisted Development from User Feedback to Production Fix

Apr 3, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Claude Code in Action: AI-Assisted Development from User Feedback to Production Fix

Section titled “Claude Code in Action: AI-Assisted Development from User Feedback to Production Fix”

A complete walkthrough of investigating, fixing, reviewing, and verifying a medical device data loss issue

Background

Section titled “Background”

Near the end of a particular month, the operations team received user feedback: two bolus delivery events from a medical CGM device (serial number EQ-7830) were not showing up in the operations management dashboard. The user provided the raw telemetry data for the two events:

This was a cross-system issue involving device data synchronization, backend deduplication logic, and frontend data display. We used Claude Code along with the BMAD Quick Dev workflow and multiple MCP Servers to complete the entire process from investigation to fix.

Phase 1: Launching the Investigation with BMAD Quick Dev

Section titled “Phase 1: Launching the Investigation with BMAD Quick Dev”

Workflow Initialization

Section titled “Workflow Initialization”

Using the /bmad-quick-dev skill, Claude Code automatically completed:

  1. Baseline commit capture: git rev-parse HEAD → e7a21f3, ensuring all subsequent changes are traceable
  2. Mode detection: Identified as Mode B (direct execution), no need to generate a technical spec first
  3. Escalation assessment: Determined to be a single bug investigation, no need to escalate to the full BMAD process

After selecting [E] Execute directly, we entered the context-gathering phase.

Code Exploration: code-explorer Sub-agent

Section titled “Code Exploration: code-explorer Sub-agent”

Claude Code launched a feature-dev:code-explorer sub-agent to perform an end-to-end trace of the entire bolus_delivery data flow:

API-side trace path:

Operations dashboard trace path:

The sub-agent read 16 key files and ultimately identified a section of code in the deduplication logic event_deduplicator.rb as the prime suspect.

Phase 2: Verifying Against Production Database via MCP

Section titled “Phase 2: Verifying Against Production Database via MCP”

Database MCP Server

Section titled “Database MCP Server”

This was the critical turning point in the investigation. By querying the production database directly through MCP, we obtained definitive evidence:

Step 1: Find the device

Step 2: Find that day’s events

The result showed only sequences 2043 and 2044—sequences 2045 and 2046 were completely missing—the events were never saved to the database at all.

Step 3: Global search by raw_payload

Found them! But the events were from roughly 2 years ago, belonging to a completely different user (owner_id: 10002, subject_id: 20001):

Event IDevent_datesequence_idvalueowner_idcreated_at
9000012024-03-1220455.0100022024-03-12
9000022024-03-1220465.0100022024-03-12

Root Cause Confirmed

Section titled “Root Cause Confirmed”

The deduplication logic (production branch):

Root cause: The medical CGM device’s sequence counter is 2 bytes (max 65535), cycling approximately every 2 years. When the counter wrapped around, it produced raw_payload telemetry frames identical to those from 2 years earlier. The deduplication query had no event_date and no time window, so the old events were falsely identified as “duplicates” of the current ones, causing the new events to be discarded.

Git History Trace

Section titled “Git History Trace”

Claude Code further traced the history of when event_date was removed:

Reason for removal: Another device (EQ-5217) was experiencing duplicate event issues. Because the parser inferred the year using Date.current (the device’s raw telemetry frames don’t include the year), multiple syncs on the same day could produce different event_date values, causing deduplication to fail. So raw_payload (the stable raw telemetry frame) was used instead of event_date.

This meant simply adding event_date back would reintroduce the old bug. A solution that addresses both problems simultaneously was needed.

Phase 3: Designing and Implementing the Fix

Section titled “Phase 3: Designing and Implementing the Fix”

Three-Layer Defense Strategy

Section titled “Three-Layer Defense Strategy”

This solution addresses both problems simultaneously:

  • Original issue (EQ-5217): Same-day duplicate syncs → raw_payload within the 1-year window still catches them
  • Current issue (EQ-7830): Sequence counter wraparound → events from ~2 years ago fall outside the 1-year window, no longer falsely matched

Phase 4: /code-review — Four-Way Parallel Adversarial Review

Section titled “Phase 4: /code-review — Four-Way Parallel Adversarial Review”

After the fix was complete, the /code-review skill launched 4 parallel review sub-agents:

Review Architecture

Section titled “Review Architecture”

Each sub-agent ran independently without interfering with the others, and the results were consolidated into a unified report.

Key Findings

Section titled “Key Findings”

Architecture review discovered that deduplication blocks for other event types contained the exact same vulnerability—3 out of 4 review sub-agents independently identified this issue, corroborating each other.

Performance review found:

  • The deduplication query lacked a composite index, causing a full table scan on every sync
  • events.present? loads all matching events into memory; .exists? should be used instead
  • 1.year.ago was being recalculated on every loop iteration

Security review found:

  • The newly added .where("events.created_at >= ?", cycle_cutoff) uses parameterized queries—safe
  • However, pre-existing SQL string interpolation risks existed in the same file

Final Fix Checklist

Section titled “Final Fix Checklist”

Based on the review findings, a total of 7 items were fixed:

#FixCategory
1bolus_delivery dedup: add event_date + time windowCore fix
2Other event type dedup: apply same fixConsistency
3Extract SEQUENCE_CYCLE_WINDOW constantMaintainability
4Pre-loop calculation of cycle_cutoffPerformance
5.present? → .exists? (3 locations)Performance
6SQL interpolation → Arel expressionsSecurity
7Add composite index (CONCURRENTLY)Performance

Phase 5: Automated Test Generation and Verification

Section titled “Phase 5: Automated Test Generation and Verification”

Test Design

Section titled “Test Design”

Claude Code automatically generated 4 integration tests covering two dimensions:

Key Points in the Test Code

Section titled “Key Points in the Test Code”

The tests needed to simulate “events from 2 years ago”:

Issues Resolved During Test Runs

Section titled “Issues Resolved During Test Runs”

  1. Docker container couldn’t connect to the test database: The container network couldn’t reach the external database. Resolved by adjusting network configuration.

  2. Pending migration: The new index migration needed to be run first. Resolved via docker exec -e RAILS_ENV=test rails db:migrate.

  3. ActionController::Parameters type mismatch: deduplicate_and_persist internally calls .permit, requiring ActionController::Parameters rather than a plain Hash. Added a to_ac_params helper method as a wrapper.

Final Result

Section titled “Final Result”

Data Safety Confirmation

Section titled “Data Safety Confirmation”

Before running the tests, the database impact was confirmed:

  • The test framework was configured with config.use_transactional_fixtures = true
  • Each test runs within a transaction that automatically rolls back when finished
  • No permanent modifications to the test database whatsoever

Phase 6: Confirming the Scope of Changes and Git Commit

Section titled “Phase 6: Confirming the Scope of Changes and Git Commit”

AI-Assisted Git Workflow

Section titled “AI-Assisted Git Workflow”

Throughout the fix process, Claude Code autonomously handled Git operations, while strictly following a “confirm before executing” principle at critical points:

1. Baseline Lock

At the start of the investigation, the BMAD Quick Dev workflow automatically captured the baseline commit. All subsequent changes were measured against this baseline, ensuring git diff could show the complete scope of the fix.

2. Safe Handling of schema

After running the migration, the database schema file was regenerated, producing thousands of lines of irrelevant diffs (the test database had an incomplete table structure). Claude Code proactively identified this risk:

Immediately reverted, not included in the commit:

3. Precise Staging and Commit

Only the 3 target files were staged, using the Conventional Commits format:

4. Push Left to Human Control

After completing the commit, Claude Code did not automatically push. Pushing to the production branch is a high-risk operation, left for the developer to confirm and execute manually.

Scope of Changes Analysis

Section titled “Scope of Changes Analysis”
FileChangesDescription
event_deduplicator.rb+19/-9Dedup logic fix + performance optimization + security hardening
add_event_dedup_index.rb+11 (new)Composite index, created CONCURRENTLY
event_deduplicator_spec.rb+225 (new)4 integration tests

Impact Assessment

Section titled “Impact Assessment”
  • Only affects the deduplication path for specific medical infusion device bolus, infusion, and alarm events
  • Not affected: Other device types, monitoring events, baseline parameter events
  • Index creation uses CONCURRENTLY: No table locks, no impact on production reads/writes

Phase 7: QA Manual Verification Checklist

Section titled “Phase 7: QA Manual Verification Checklist”

A concise verification checklist was produced for the QA team:

  1. Re-sync the device: Have the target device re-sync; the previously missing events should now appear in the operations dashboard
  2. Dedup still works: Sync again; no duplicates should appear
  3. Regression check: Pick an older device that’s been in use for over a year and confirm events look normal
  4. Operations dashboard verification path: Subject → Data table → Filter by event type → That day should have complete data

Phase 8: Device-Side Log Verification — Closing the Loop

Section titled “Phase 8: Device-Side Log Verification — Closing the Loop”

The code and database investigation had already pinpointed the root cause, but a complete closed loop required the full log chain from device to server to ultimately confirm the issue reported by the user. Using the log aggregation system, we were able to reconstruct the complete chain of events.

Client App Side

Section titled “Client App Side”

The client app is the mobile application through which users interact with the medical device. After a user performs an action in the app, it reads the latest events from the device via BLE Bluetooth and uploads them to the server through the TelemetrySyncWorker.

Logs confirmed:

  • The app did read the missing events from the device
  • BLE communication was normal, telemetry frames were complete
  • The parsed raw_payload matched the user’s report exactly

Server API Side

Section titled “Server API Side”

After the server received the sync request, it entered the EventService.deduplicate_and_persist processing flow. Production logs clearly recorded the deduplication decision:

Irrefutable evidence:

  • The dedup query matched events from approximately 2 years ago
  • After matching, next was executed—both new events were skipped and never saved

Telemetry Gateway Side

Section titled “Telemetry Gateway Side”

In addition to the client’s active sync, the telemetry gateway also periodically collects device data automatically. Logs showed the telemetry side was similarly blocked by the old events—regardless of how the user synced, the problem would reproduce.

Complete Log Chain — Closed Loop

Section titled “Complete Log Chain — Closed Loop”

Expected Behavior After Fix

Section titled “Expected Behavior After Fix”

After deploying the fix, the dedup query will include event_date and a created_at time window constraint. Old events won’t match due to date mismatch and falling outside the 1-year window, so they’ll no longer be falsely identified as duplicates, and new events will be saved normally.

Toolchain and Workflow Summary

Section titled “Toolchain and Workflow Summary”

BMAD Quick Dev Workflow

Section titled “BMAD Quick Dev Workflow”

MCP Server Collaboration

Section titled “MCP Server Collaboration”
MCP ServerPurpose
Database MCPProduction database queries: confirm event status, device info, locate old events
Logs MCPDevice sync log queries: reconstruct full chain across client/telemetry/API

Sub-agent Orchestration

Section titled “Sub-agent Orchestration”
Sub-agentTypePurpose
code-explorerfeature-dev:code-explorerEnd-to-end data flow tracing (16 files)
arch-reviewcode-review-expertArchitectural consistency review
quality-reviewcode-review-expertCode quality review
perf-reviewcode-review-expertPerformance and scalability review
security-reviewcode-review-expertSecurity review

Key Numbers

Section titled “Key Numbers”
  • From investigation to root cause: Located ~2-year-old events in 3 SQL queries
  • Review findings: 4 sub-agents independently identified 7 issues
  • Fix scope: 1 file logic change + 1 index migration + 1 test file
  • Test coverage: 4 integration tests covering both new-event-passes and duplicate-event-blocked dimensions
  • Data safety: Transactional tests, zero permanent data modifications

Lessons Learned

Section titled “Lessons Learned”

  1. MCP access to the production database is an investigation accelerator. Three SQL queries pinpointed the root cause, saving enormous amounts of guesswork and log searching.

  2. Git history tracing is not optional. event_date was removed for a reason—adding it back without understanding the history would have reintroduced the old bug.

  3. Parallel adversarial reviews catch blind spots. Three out of four independent review sub-agents discovered the same vulnerability in other event types—something easily missed in a single-person review.

  4. Automated tests should simulate real-world scenarios. Using 2.years.ago to simulate old events and the current date for new events precisely covered the time window boundary conditions.

  5. Confirm data safety before applying fixes. Tests run within transactions that auto-rollback, and the migration uses CONCURRENTLY to avoid table locks—zero risk to production.

Fixing Garbled CJK Characters After SSH Login on macOS

Apr 3, 2026
Vibe Sparking

The Problem

Section titled “The Problem”

After SSH-ing into a macOS host, viewing Markdown files containing CJK (Chinese/Japanese/Korean) characters with more shows garbled text or a binary file warning:

Even when you choose to view it anyway, CJK characters display as garbled text.

Root Cause

Section titled “Root Cause”

Checking the locale settings on the remote host:

LANG is empty and all LC_* variables are set to C.

The C locale only recognizes single-byte ASCII characters. UTF-8 encoded CJK characters use 3 bytes each, which under the C locale are treated as illegal byte sequences. This causes:

  • more to misidentify the file as binary
  • cat to output garbled text (depending on whether the terminal emulator handles UTF-8 independently)
  • less may partially work (it has its own character encoding logic)

Why Does macOS Behave This Way?

Section titled “Why Does macOS Behave This Way?”

macOS Terminal.app has “Set locale environment variables on startup” enabled by default, so local sessions get LANG set to en_US.UTF-8 or zh_CN.UTF-8. However, when connecting via SSH:

  1. The SSH client may not forward locale variables (depends on SendEnv config)
  2. The remote sshd may not accept locale variables (depends on AcceptEnv config)
  3. The user’s shell config (.zshrc / .bashrc) doesn’t explicitly set LANG

If any of these conditions fails, the remote session falls back to the C locale.

The Fix

Section titled “The Fix”

The most reliable approach: explicitly set the locale in the remote host’s shell config file.

This doesn’t depend on SSH locale forwarding and works regardless of how you connect.

Steps

Section titled “Steps”

Check the default shell on the remote host:

Add to the end of the appropriate file:

We use en_US.UTF-8 rather than zh_CN.UTF-8 because macOS ships with en_US.UTF-8 out of the box — no extra locale generation needed. If you need Chinese sorting and date formats, zh_CN.UTF-8 works too (also built into macOS).

Verification

Section titled “Verification”

After reconnecting via SSH:

Try viewing CJK files again:

Bulk Checking Multiple Hosts

Section titled “Bulk Checking Multiple Hosts”

If you manage multiple machines, a one-liner to check them all:

Any output showing LANG="" or LANG="C" needs fixing.

Bulk fix:

Real-World Example

Section titled “Real-World Example”

We investigated this issue across several hosts:

HostOSLANG Before FixNeeds Fix?
cloud-server-1Debian (Cloud)C.UTF-8❌ Already UTF-8
linux-device-1Debian (ARM)en_GB.UTF-8❌ Already UTF-8
mac-host-1macOS (Intel)"" (empty)✅
mac-host-2macOS (Intel)"" (empty)✅
mac-host-3macOS (M1)"" (empty)✅

The pattern is clear: Linux hosts come with UTF-8 locale configured by default; macOS hosts do not.

Additional Tips

Section titled “Additional Tips”
  1. Prefer less over more — less handles UTF-8 more robustly and often displays correctly even with broken locale settings
  2. Don’t rely on SSH locale forwarding — SendEnv / AcceptEnv configurations are inconsistent across systems; explicit settings are most reliable
  3. LC_CTYPE is the key variable — if you can only set one, make it LC_CTYPE=en_US.UTF-8; it controls character classification and encoding detection

Summary

Section titled “Summary”

When macOS serves as an SSH server, it doesn’t set any locale environment variables by default. Local usage is unaffected (Terminal.app sets them automatically), but SSH remote sessions fall back to the C locale, causing CJK and other multi-byte characters to display incorrectly. Adding export LANG=en_US.UTF-8 to your shell config file solves this completely.

Global App Store Price Comparison Guide: Same Subscription, Over 60% Price Difference

Apr 3, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Did you know? The same Claude Pro subscription costs over 60% less when purchased from the Nigerian App Store compared to the UK. This isn’t a bug — it’s how Apple’s global pricing system works.

How Does Apple’s “Regional Pricing” Work?

Section titled “How Does Apple’s “Regional Pricing” Work?”

Apple sets different price tiers for App Stores across 175 countries and regions. Developers choose a base price, and Apple automatically generates regional prices based on exchange rates, tax rates, and local purchasing power. But this automatic conversion isn’t always precise — currency fluctuations, tax differences, and Apple’s deliberate “psychological pricing” strategies create significant price gaps for the same app across different countries.

This creates an information asymmetry: if you know which region is cheapest, you could theoretically save a considerable amount on subscription fees.

App Store Price: A Global Comparison Tool at a Glance

Section titled “App Store Price: A Global Comparison Tool at a Glance”

App Store Price was built to solve exactly this problem. It scrapes App Store in-app purchase and subscription prices from major regions worldwide, converts them to a single currency, and lets you see at a glance where things are cheapest — and most expensive.

Core Features

Section titled “Core Features”
  • Real-time global price comparison: Covers major App Store regions with prices converted to a unified currency
  • Price rankings: Sorted from lowest to highest, the cheapest region is immediately obvious
  • Visual charts: Horizontal bar charts for intuitive price distribution visualization
  • Popular app coverage: From Claude and ChatGPT to Netflix, YouTube, and Spotify — major paid apps and services are all included
  • Companion iOS app (Pinlist): Real-time price alerts and tracking

Website: https://appstoreprice.org

Real-World Example: Claude Subscription Global Pricing

Section titled “Real-World Example: Claude Subscription Global Pricing”

Taking Anthropic’s Claude App (iOS) Claude Max 20x 1M plan as an example, here are the prices scraped from various regions (converted to CNY):

RankCountry/RegionPrice (CNY)Notes
1🇳🇬 Nigeria¥998.72Global lowest
2🇪🇬 Egypt¥1,157.12
3🇵🇰 Pakistan¥1,505.54
4🇹🇷 Turkey¥1,545.76
5🇻🇳 Vietnam¥1,628.41
6🇰🇷 South Korea—
7🇦🇷 Argentina—
8🇺🇸 United States—Developer base price
………
19🇬🇧 United Kingdom—Global highest

The bar chart clearly shows a significant gap between Nigeria (green, lowest) and the UK (red, highest). The US, as the developer base price region, sits roughly in the upper-middle range.

Interesting Findings

Section titled “Interesting Findings”
  1. Africa and South Asia are typically cheapest: Nigeria, Egypt, and Pakistan consistently rank in the top three for lowest prices
  2. Turkey remains a bargain hunter’s paradise: Despite multiple Apple price adjustments, Turkey’s prices remain highly competitive
  3. European regions are generally expensive: Germany, France, and the UK include higher VAT rates, pushing prices well above the US
  4. Japan, Taiwan, and Australia sit at moderate levels
  5. Not available in mainland China: The Claude App is currently not offered on the mainland China App Store

What Else Can This Tool Show?

Section titled “What Else Can This Tool Show?”

The homepage features price comparison entries for numerous popular apps across multiple categories:

  • AI Tools: Claude, ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Grok, Kimi, Manus
  • Streaming: Netflix, Disney+, YouTube, Spotify, Apple Music, bilibili, iQIYI
  • Utilities: 1Password, Notion, Goodnotes, Duolingo, Termius
  • Proxy/Network Tools: Shadowrocket, Surge 5, Loon, Quantumult X, Stash, Egern
  • Cloud Storage: iCloud, Google One, OneDrive, Baidu Netdisk, PikPak
  • Games: Genshin Impact, Minecraft

Each app page shows how many subscription plans are available for comparison. For instance, YouTube has up to 46 plans, Google One has 21, and Disney+ has 28 — all with per-region pricing you can browse individually.

Practical Considerations

Section titled “Practical Considerations”

Before you excitedly switch your App Store region, here are a few things to know:

⚠️ Region Switching Has Barriers

Section titled “⚠️ Region Switching Has Barriers”
  • You need a payment method for the target region (some regions allow registration without payment, but subscriptions require valid payment)
  • Existing subscriptions don’t automatically migrate when you switch regions
  • Some apps may not be available in certain regions

⚠️ Exchange Rate Fluctuations

Section titled “⚠️ Exchange Rate Fluctuations”
  • The website shows prices based on real-time exchange rates; actual charges may vary
  • Some credit cards charge foreign transaction fees

⚠️ Apple May Adjust Prices

Section titled “⚠️ Apple May Adjust Prices”
  • Apple periodically adjusts regional price tiers
  • Previously ultra-cheap regions (like Argentina and Turkey) have already gone through multiple rounds of price increases

✅ Smart Usage

Section titled “✅ Smart Usage”
  • Family sharing plans also work in low-price regions, offering even better value
  • Gift cards can further reduce costs

Conclusion

Section titled “Conclusion”

App Store Price is a clean, practical comparison tool, especially useful for:

  • Heavy subscribers: Managing multiple subscriptions adds up — price comparison saves real money
  • Developers: Understanding your app’s pricing distribution across global regions to optimize pricing strategy
  • The curious: Simply wanting to know “how much does the same thing cost around the world”

In an era of ubiquitous digital subscriptions, price differences for the same service across markets can easily exceed 50%. This tool won’t save you all your money, but at least it lets you know how much extra you’re paying before you commit.

Data source: App Store Price, prices based on April 2026 real-time exchange rates, for reference only.
